title: Tell me about a time you mentored or developed someone
prompt: Tell me about a time you helped someone learn or develop a skill. Explain what they wanted help with, what you did and what changed. The example can be informal, and you do not need to identify the person or describe a promotion.
blurb: Mentoring: did they invest in someone's growth and see real development — or just answer questions?

rubric.label: The person & their need
rubric.description: Explains a specific learning need and how it was understood, without requiring personal details, a career step or a formal mentoring role.

rubric.label: Investing in their growth
rubric.description: Explains their responsibility and how the help respected the learner’s goals, preferences and boundaries.

rubric.label: Specific contribution and decisions
rubric.description: Describes specific support, feedback, demonstration or practice and how it was adapted; doing part of a task can be appropriate when explained.

rubric.label: Outcome and evidence
rubric.description: Describes the learner’s observed progress or remaining difficulty using qualitative or quantitative evidence and gives the learner proper credit.

rubric.label: Reflection & adapting
rubric.description: Explains what they learned about adapting support and how they would check whether a future approach is useful.

rubric.label: Clear, relevant communication
rubric.description: Makes the relevant situation, reasoning and contribution understandable in any clear order. No required STAR structure, pronouns, performance of confidence or emotional tone.

reference.scenario: Explore helping someone learn in a class, shift, community activity or professional setting. Small skill gains and informal help count. Assess responsiveness to the learner, useful actions and evidence of learning without requiring a promotion or judging confidence from appearance.
model_points: Checks what the learner wants or needs rather than assuming a deficit.
Explains the candidate’s role and what support was appropriate.
Uses a specific explanation, demonstration, practice opportunity or feedback suited to the task.
Checks understanding and adapts when the approach is not helping.
Describes progress or remaining difficulty with honest evidence; the learner retains credit for their work.
Identifies a lesson about providing support and knowing when another source of help is needed.

probes.question: How did you find out what help the person wanted?

probes.trigger: candidate says only that they showed someone
probes.question: What did you do to check their understanding?
What could you actually observe them doing afterward?

red_flags: Claims the learner’s work as their own achievement.
Continues an approach despite clear evidence it is harmful or ignores the learner’s stated boundaries.
Treats an assumption about confidence or identity as proof of ability.
follow_ups: What did you change when the first explanation did not help?
When would you seek another source of support?
reference.exemplar_answer: Illustrative example only; it is not a required setting, answer order or achievement standard. A new volunteer wanted to learn our filing process. I asked which part was confusing, demonstrated one example and let them try the next while I watched. They could choose the right folder but were unsure about duplicates, so we wrote a short check for that step. They handled the next few examples independently. I cannot claim they mastered every case, but the check helped with the task we practiced.
reference.assessment_contract: Assess the selected competency from concrete job-relevant evidence. Examples from paid work, study, volunteering, caregiving, informal work, military service and community activities are equally eligible when relevant. A modest example is sufficient if it shows the competency; employer prestige, formal title and financial scale are not criteria. Accept qualitative or quantitative outcomes supported by the account, including partial or unsuccessful outcomes. Do not require a numeric metric, STAR order, particular pronouns, composure, enthusiasm or a particular communication style. Identify personal contribution by meaning while preserving credit to others. Assess intelligibility and relevance, not accent, fluency, verbosity, visible emotion, disability or private circumstances. Mark genuinely missing evidence not assessed; do not infer poor competence or dishonesty from an absent example. A clearly labeled hypothetical may be discussed as situational practice but must not count as demonstrated past experience. Respect scope of practice, authorization, safety and ethical duties; pausing, declining, reporting or escalating can be sound judgment. Never require obedience, direct confrontation, unpaid overwork or successful persuasion regardless of the circumstances.
